title: The ePrint:2026/1591 Quantum Algorithm Does Not Solve DCP
authors: Aparna Gupte, Seyoon Ragavan, and Mark Zhandry
abstract:
In this note, we formally show that the recent algorithm by Simon (ePrint:2026/1591, August 11 2026) does not extract the least-significant bit of the dihedral coset problem (DCP) secret with non-negligible guessing advantage, and therefore does not solve DCP. We emphasize that our result is not merely about Simon's analysis of his algorithm; we are showing directly that the algorithm cannot possibly work.

Our no-go encompasses a much broader class of algorithms than the specific algorithm by Simon. The main message of our no-go is that an algorithm for DCP following the template of the reduction by Regev (SIAM Journal on Computing, 2004) will probably have to make extensive use of the classical Fourier labels in the uncomputation stage. On the other hand, the algorithm by Simon can be implemented, up to error $\mathsf{poly}(n)2^{-n/3}$, using only the most-significant third of the classical Fourier labels, and therefore cannot succeed.

To help with verifiability, we release Lean 4 code for our results, available at https://github.com/sragavan99/lean-ePrint-2026-1591-refutation.

                   Aparna Gupte                    Seyoon Ragavan                     Mark Zhandry

                                                                 Abstract
            In this note, we formally show that the recent algorithm by Simon (ePrint:2026/1591, August 11 2026) does
        not extract the least-significant bit of the dihedral coset problem (DCP) secret with non-negligible guessing advan-
        tage, and therefore does not solve DCP. We emphasize that our result is not merely about Simon’s analysis of his
        algorithm; we are showing directly that the algorithm cannot possibly work.
            Our no-go encompasses a much broader class of algorithms than the specific algorithm by Simon. The main
        message of our no-go is that an algorithm for DCP following the template of the reduction by Regev (SIAM Journal
        on Computing, 2004) will probably have to make extensive use of the classical Fourier labels in the uncomputation
        stage. On the other hand, the algorithm by Simon can be implemented, up to error poly(n)2−n/3 , using only the
        most-significant third of the classical Fourier labels, and therefore cannot succeed.
            To help with verifiability, we release Lean 4 code for our results, available at this GitHub repository.


1      Introduction
Recently, Simon [Sim26] claimed a quantum polynomial-time (QPT) algorithm for the dihedral coset problem (DCP).
By an existing reduction due to Regev [Reg04], such an algorithm would imply a QPT algorithm for hard lattice
problems. Such an algorithm would undermine the security claims of proposed post-quantum lattice-based cryp-
tosystems.
    (Un)fortunately, we demonstrate that Simon’s new algorithm cannot actually efficiently solve DCP, and therefore
does not efficiently solve hard lattice problems nor undermine the security of lattice-based cryptosystems. We do
so by examining a general blueprint followed by both Regev and Simon, and show that if too much information is
discarded during the course of the algorithm, then the algorithm cannot succeed in solving DCP. We then explain
that Simon’s algorithm indeed discards too much information, and therefore Simon’s algorithm cannot succeed.
    While our initial motivation was to analyze Simon’s algorithm, our no-go result is very general, and may help
guide future efforts to develop quantum algorithms for DCP or related problems such as lattices.

Organization. We first recall the proposed algorithm of Simon [Sim26] in Section 1.1, give intuition for why this
algorithm should not work in Section 1.2, and state the formal impossibility, the main result, in Section 1.3. A brief
background is given in Section 2. The proofs are in Section 3.

1.2     Intuition for the No-Go
Before we formally state our no-go results, we provide some intuition for them.
    To start, consider the state after Step 2. Suppose we measured the b register, collapsing it into a classical state.
Since the secret d lives in the phase of this state, collapsing the b register would lose all information about d to the
global phase. Maintaining coherence across different values of b is therefore crucial to recovering d. In fact,
we want to make this coherence computationally accessible—this is what Regev’s algorithm [Reg04] does, assuming
a subset-sum oracle.
   2 Simon’s manuscript [Sim26] uses z′ instead of z to denote the measurement result.




                                                                                 2
    Our observation is that Simon’s algorithm [Sim26] actually effectively loses the coherence, meaning it cannot
recover any information about the secret d.
    In more detail, we observe that Simon’s algorithm [Sim26] is essentially equivalent to an alternate algorithm
that discards many bits of each y after Step 2. What we show is that, by averaging over the discarded bits of y,
the resulting state fails to maintain coherence across different values of b. As such, any possible algorithm that
doesn’t make use of the discarded bits of y simply cannot recover any information about d.

A Toy Example. To build intuition, consider for a moment an algorithm that stops making use of y, z after Step 2.
(We emphasize that this is not what [Sim26] is doing; we only start with this setting to build intuition.) If this were
the case, then the algorithm’s success would not be affected by instead discarding the y, z classical registers in their
entirety. We can then compute the density matrix for the mixed state obtained by averaging over the discarded bits:

In this hypothetical scenario, the algorithm must recover d from this mixed state.
     We claim that this state has negligible trace distance from the state obtained by simply measuring the b register.
To see this, observe that outside the point b = 0, the function fy1 is a pairwise independent function if y is sampled
randomly. The only exception to pairwise independence is the fact that fy1 (0) = 0. For each (b, b′ ) pair (excluding 0),
over the choice of y, the probability that (b, b′ ) remain coherent is exponentially small. Since y has been discarded
and we average over the choice of y, we find that the resulting density matrix has all off-diagonal terms exponen-
tially suppressed. A direct calculation shows that the resulting density matrix is exponentially-close to the diagonal
matrix–that is, the diagonal mixed state where the b’s are totally decohered. We additionally need to handle the
terms where b = 0, but since these have an exponentially-small mass, it does not significantly change the outcome.
Thus, all information about d is lost, except with exponentially-small probability.
     A less precise version of the above intuition is the following: consider a purification of the algorithm that holds y
in superposition. Then the y register is very strongly entangled with the b register. If these registers were maximally
entangled, then discarding the y register has the effect of completely decohering the b register. So if the registers
were instead just strongly entangled, then discarding the y register should still have a strong decoherence effect on
the b register.


Applying to Simon’s actual algorithm. Simon’s algorithm [Sim26] does not discard y at Step 2, and actually
uses y in Step 3. After Step 3, y is never used again, so it can be considered discarded immediately after Step 3.
     Despite not discarding y until after Step 3, a more refined version of the argument above shows that the amount
of information about y that is actually used in Step 3 is not enough to keep the b register usefully coherent. We
formalize this using “digest functions” Hi : ZN → [K] for i ∈ [m] that can be used to retain some information about
y and discard the rest. Our main theorem shows that, if the digest functions have small enough outputs, it remains
the case that d is statistically hidden, even given the outputs of the digest function.
     We then observe that in Step 3 of the algorithm by [Sim26], y is only used to compute the functions gy(i) (b(i) ),
which recall are the log n most-significant bits of the inner-product of y(i) and b(i) . Since the b(i) are small, changing
the least-significant bits of y(i) only slightly changes the inner-product, which means that the output of g is unaffected
(with high probability). As such, we can actually compute g, and hence the state in Step 3, only given, say, the top
third most significant bits of y, discarding the least significant two-thirds as well as z.3 The top-third of the bits of y
is a sufficiently small digest of y for our theorem to apply. Due to the chance that low-order bits cause a large cascade
of carries, our implementation using the top-third of the bits of y does incur a tiny statistical error of poly(n)2−n/3 ,
but this does not change the final result that all information about d is hidden.
  3 Discarding the lower two-thirds of y is in fact sufficient, and even if the algorithm additionally depended on z it would not help.

1.4     Remarks
Remark 1.3 (Very superficial circumventions that do not salvage the algorithm). Theorem 1.1 admits some very
superficial circumventions by modifying the algorithm to retain a register containing y (but not actually use this register
in any way), or to postpone the measurement of y until the end of the algorithm. In fact, the algorithm by Simon [Sim26]
appears to do this at the surface since it only measures y at the end of Step 4.
    The specific tweaks described above do not protect the algorithm from our no-go results, because we can switch to an
alternative algorithm that (a) is covered by Theorem 1.1; and (b) has exactly the same output distribution (in terms of
the single-bit guess for LSB(d)) as the original algorithm. Such an alternative algorithm can be obtained by discarding
registers after the algorithm operates on them for the last time, and commuting the measurement of y to the end of Step 1
(using the fact that we are only commuting this measurement past operations that control on the standard-basis contents
of the y register).
Remark 1.4 (Post-selection technicalities). Strictly speaking, the algorithm by [Sim26] involves several runs, for both
of the following reasons:
      • To retry if one of the measurements in the later steps of the algorithm by [Sim26] does not succeed. In this case,
        the run would output restart; or
      • To amplify the purported reliability of the algorithm’s guess in {0, 1} for the least-significant bit of the secret d.
The algorithm terminates when sufficiently-many runs output a bit instead of restart. Without analyzing the remaining
steps of the algorithm by [Sim26], we need to be careful to show that the additional runs do not circumvent Corollary 1.2,
which only applies to a single run.
    First, notice that if each run outputs restart with probability 1, then the expected run-time is infinite. Therefore, we
assume the probability of restart is strictly less than 1. In this case, the algorithm will terminate with probability 1 and
output a bit.
    We next derive from Corollary 1.2 that there are only two possibilities: either the algorithm is simply incorrect, or
the algorithm fails to run in even sub-exponential time. This can be shown in a standard way as follows: fix two secrets


                                                                      4
d0 , d1 with opposite least-significant bits, and consider a formally truncated version of the algorithm that is allowed at
most 2⌊2n/9⌋ runs, returning an arbitrary fixed bit if the algorithm has not decided its single-bit output by this point.
These 2⌊2n/9⌋ runs should encompass both retries and amplification. We now have a win-win argument:
    • By Corollary 1.2 and a standard hybrid argument, the formally truncated algorithm distinguishes the LSB(d) = 0
      and LSB(d) = 1 cases with advantage at most

                                                22n/9 · poly(n)2−n/3 ≤ poly(n)2−n/9 .

    • Suppose that, for at least one i ∈ {0, 1}, the eventual output distribution on secret di has statistical distance at least
      2−n/9 from its formally truncated output distribution. These distributions can differ only if the algorithm has not
      finished after 2⌊2n/9⌋ runs. Consequently, that event has probability at least 2−n/9 , and the expected number of runs
      on secret di is at least
                                                       2−n/9 · 2⌊2n/9⌋ ≥ 2n/9−1 .
      Otherwise, for both secrets the eventual distribution is within 2−n/9 of its truncated distribution. The triangle
      inequality then shows that the two eventual output distributions have statistical distance at most

                                             poly(n)2−n/9 + 2 · 2−n/9 = poly(n)2−n/9 .

Thus, either the algorithm has expected runtime Ω(2n/9 ) for at least one of the two secrets, or its eventual distinguishing
advantage between the two secrets is at most poly(n)2−n/9 . In particular, it cannot simultaneously have subexponential
expected runtime and inverse-subexponential correctness advantage.
Remark 1.5. We remark that our no-go captures a broader class of algorithms than [Sim26] in two ways:
   1. First, we rule out algorithms that retain arbitrary small digests, not just the first few MSBs of blockwise subset
      sums gy(i) that are used in [Sim26].
   2. Second, we do not require that the algorithm discard z = fy1 (b) value; our no-go holds even if further operations
      that are classically controlled on this register are performed, as long as the z register is collapsed. Simon’s algorithm
      ignores the z register after Step 2, so it effectively measures and discards this register.

Outlook and caveats. Eliding some technical details, the algorithm by [Reg04] follows Steps 1 and 2 but then
uses a subset-sum oracle to coherently erase the |b⟩ register, given the subset sum ⟨b, y⟩ mod N = z + hN/2 as input.
Implementing such a subset-sum oracle (inefficiently) requires the algorithm to use the classical information y, z in
its entirety. The qualitative takeaway from Theorem 1.1 is that this is an inherent requirement not just for Regev’s
algorithm but for any algorithm that picks up from step 2; even discarding as few as ω(log n) bits of each yi in a
predetermined way is enough to information-theoretically hide the least-significant bit of d.
     Our result is best viewed as a rigorous refutation of the specific algorithm by [Sim26], as well as a guide impos-
ing some constraints on a hypothetical repaired algorithm (subject to following the broad template of [Reg04]). We
anticipate that there might be variants of the algorithm by [Sim26] that circumvent the formal scope of Theorem 1.1
(in ways less trivial than described in Remark 1.3), but in superficial ways that do not salvage the algorithm’s correct-
ness. There is the possibility of a genuine and plausible repair path that circumvents Theorem 1.1 in a meaningful
way, but we are not aware of such an approach.
